title: Add approve/reject by id for steward work-item proposals
summary: Add `athena approve-work <id>` and `athena reject-work <id> --why`, which decide a pending steward work item (kind proposal) by its id, mirroring accept-proposal/reject-proposal. Approving submits an ordinary job whose request text inlines the work item's title, rung, source and the content of each cited record, because readers can't see records/. The audience is the user who approves proposals. The decision is appended as a new record, since work items are never edited.

defaults_applied.how: All new code is Rust in the existing crates.
New record type and both commands get passing tests; clippy is clean.
Docs and CHANGELOG explain the commands for an outside reader.
The fix is that the request carries the work item's content. It does not point the user at a path or give readers special access.
One focused change that mirrors the existing proposal flow.
Behavior is checked by cargo test on the CLI path.
The work-item vs defaults-proposal meaning and the missing request text were recovered from steward.rs and proposals.rs.
BRIEF.md asks for tagged releases and a changelog, so the change records itself in CHANGELOG.md.

assumptions: 'Steward proposal' means a WorkItem of kind Proposal: a change above the steward's ladder limit, queued only as a work item. It is not the defaults proposal that accept-proposal already handles.
A WorkItem stores no request text (ProposedChange.request is dropped in decide), so the request for the approved job is built from the item's title, rung, source and evidence.

The approved request must carry the cited content itself, such as the cited jobs' requests and outcomes and the source's text. A bare path like records/work-items/... is exactly what produced the blind reading.

Work items are never edited, so approval or rejection is a new appended record that links the work-item id to the job or to the reason. A new record schema is acceptable, with its path, validation and round-trip test following the existing record pattern.
Approving goes through the usual `ask` reading flow, like accept_proposal. Only open items can be decided, and an item already decided is refused.
The CLI surface is two new subcommands beside AcceptProposal and RejectProposal. Their exact names are the producer's call.

acceptance_criteria.text: Reading the request built for an approved work item shows the item's title, rung, source and evidence, plus the content of each cited record inlined as text. The request contains no bare reference to a records/ path as the only description of the work.

A new appended record type (schema, canonical path, validation) holds a work-item decision: approved with a job id, or rejected with a non-empty reason. A work item that has a decision is no longer open, and the store loads these records.

athena-cli has new subcommands to approve and to reject a work item by id. They appear in the CLI help, and `athena status` or an equivalent output lists open work-item proposals with their ids so the user can find one.

Run `cargo test`. New tests pass: approving a seeded proposal-kind work item queues a job whose request text contains the inlined content of its cited evidence. Rejecting records the reason. A second decision, an unknown id, and an empty reason are each refused.
Run `cargo clippy --all-targets` and `cargo fmt --check`. Both are clean.
docs and CHANGELOG.md describe the new commands and say the decision is recorded as an append-only record.

out_of_scope: Changing the defaults-proposal commands (accept-proposal, reject-proposal, check-proposal).
Giving readers access to records/ in general; only the approved request carries the needed content.
Changing the steward's model, prompts, or what it queues.
Editing existing work-item records or backfilling decisions for old items.
Changes to athena.toml, defaults.toml, or workflows.
departures: Larger than typical: it needs a new record type plus CLI wiring and content inlining across several crates, so cost and time are above the reference and the pass probability is slightly lower.
